entities.name: James III of Majorca
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
James III, known as James the Rash, was the last independent King of Majorca, reigning from 1324 until 1344. Born in Catania, Sicily, in 1315, as the son of Ferdinand of Majorca and Isabella of Sabran, he inherited a complex geopolitical position. His reign was primarily defined by the relentless expansionist policies of Peter IV of Aragon, which ultimately led to the absorption of the Kingdom of Majorca into the Crown of Aragon, thereby ending a distinct cadet branch of the House of Barcelona that had ruled the Balearic Islands and continental territories since 1276.

James III's efforts to assert his kingdom's sovereignty were met with increasing pressure from his Aragonese suzerain. Despite attempts at diplomatic maneuvering and military preparations, Majorca's financial weakness, exacerbated by its obligation to pay homage to Aragon, hindered effective resistance. A pivotal moment occurred in 1342 when James III minted his own coinage, a symbolic act of defiance against Peter IV's authority, which was interpreted as a direct challenge to Aragonese feudal overlordship. This provoked an immediate and decisive military response: Peter IV's forces swiftly conquered the Balearic Islands in 1343 and the Rousillon and Cerdanya territories in 1344, formally annexing the Kingdom of Majorca.

Stripped of his domains, James III sought support from various European powers, including Philip VI of France and Pope Clement VI. In a desperate bid to reclaim his lost kingdom, he sold the strategically important city of Montpellier to France in 1349 to finance a mercenary army. He launched an invasion of Majorca, hoping for local support, but was decisively defeated and killed by Peter IV's forces at the Battle of Llucmajor on November 2, 1349. His death marked the definitive end of Majorca's independence and solidified the Crown of Aragon's control over a crucial part of the western Mediterranean.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: James III's reign and defeat fundamentally reshaped the political map of the western Mediterranean, leading to the permanent absorption of the Kingdom of Majorca into the Crown of Aragon and solidifying Aragonese maritime power for centuries.
